paragraphs: Man seems to have a lazy inclination to let long-established custom always take the place of reason, and to rest every duty on an arbitrary foundation. The rights of kings are traced in a direct line from the King of kings, and those of parents from our first parent.

Why do we reach so far back for principles that ought always to rest on the same foundation and carry the same weight today as they did a thousand years ago, and not one jot more? If parents do their duty, they have a strong hold on their children’s gratitude and a sacred claim to it; but few parents are willing to accept the respectful affection of their offspring on such terms. They demand blind obedience because they do not deserve a reasonable service; and to make these demands of weakness and ignorance more binding, a mysterious sanctity is cast around the most arbitrary of principles. For what else can we call the blind duty of obeying vicious or weak beings merely because they obeyed a powerful instinct? The reciprocal duty that naturally exists between parent and child can be defined simply, in a few words: the parent who gives proper care to a helpless infant has the right to demand the same care when the feebleness of old age comes upon him. But to subject a rational being to the mere will of another, once he is old enough to answer to society for his own conduct, is a most cruel and unwarranted stretch of power; and it is perhaps as harmful to morality as those religious systems which allow right and wrong no existence except in the will of God.

I have never known a parent who paid more than ordinary attention to his children to be disregarded by them (Dr. Johnson makes the same observation). On the contrary, the early habit of relying almost unquestioningly on the opinion of a respected parent is not easily shaken, even when mature reason has convinced the child that his father is not the wisest man in the world. A reasonable man must harden himself against this weakness, for it is a weakness, though the epithet AMIABLE may be attached to it. The absurd duty, too often instilled, of obeying a parent simply because he is a parent fetters the mind and prepares it to submit slavishly to any power except reason.
I distinguish between the natural duty owed to parents and the incidental one.

The parent who diligently tries to form his child’s heart and enlarge its understanding has given to the performance of a duty shared by the whole animal world a dignity that only reason can give. This is humane parental affection, and it leaves instinctive natural affection far behind. Such a parent acquires all the rights of the most sacred friendship, and his advice, even when his child is well on in life, deserves serious consideration.

As for marriage, although after the age of twenty-one a parent seems to have no right to withhold his consent for any reason, twenty years of anxious care still call for some return; and if the son’s choice does not fully win the approval of his first friend, the son ought at least to promise not to marry for two or three years.

But respect for parents is, generally speaking, a far more degrading principle; it is merely a selfish respect for property. The father who is obeyed blindly is obeyed out of sheer weakness, or from motives that debase human character.

It is generally admitted that a great share of the misery that roams the world in hideous forms arises from the negligence of parents; and yet these are the very people who cling most stubbornly to what they call a natural right, though it overturns the birthright of man, the right to act as his own reason directs.

I have already had frequent occasion to observe that vicious or lazy people are always eager to profit by enforcing arbitrary privileges, and generally in the same proportion as they neglect to carry out the duties that alone make those privileges reasonable. At bottom this is a dictate of common sense, or the instinct of self-defence peculiar to ignorant weakness. It resembles the instinct that makes a fish muddy the water it swims in to escape its enemy, instead of boldly facing it in the clear stream.

From the clear stream of argument, indeed, the defenders of established custom of every kind take flight; and, sheltering in the darkness that sublime poetry has imagined surrounding the throne of the Almighty, they dare to demand the unquestioning respect that is owed only to His unsearchable ways. But let me not be thought presumptuous. The darkness that hides our God from us concerns only speculative truths; it never obscures moral ones. Those shine clearly, for God is light, and by the constitution of our nature He never requires us to perform a duty whose reasonableness does not shine upon us when we open our eyes.
